Label: Normal range 36.5–37.5 °C (97.7–99.5 °F)
What it means / what to do: Within the range StatPearls gives for a normal value.
Verbatim fragment: The normal value ranges from 36.5 °C to 37.5 °C.
Note: °F values are the exact conversions; the source publishes °C only.

Label: About 36.4 °C (97.5 °F)
What it means / what to do: NHS describes this as a normal temperature in babies and children; it can vary slightly.
Source: NHS — How to take your baby's temperature
Verbatim fragment: A normal temperature in babies and children is about 36.4C, but this can vary slightly.
Note: NHS does not publish a normal range for adults; it only says normal temperature differs per person and changes during the day.

Label: Mean 36.57 °C; mean ± 2 SD 35.73–37.41 °C
What it means / what to do: Use the interval, not 37.0, when judging whether a single oral reading is unusual.
Verbatim fragment: oral is 36.57 degrees C (97.83 degrees F)
Note: c_min/c_max are mean ± 2 SD from the underlying review; the mean is in the label.

Label: Mean 37.04 °C; mean ± 2 SD 36.32–37.76 °C
What it means / what to do: Rectal readings run higher than oral ones; do not apply an oral threshold to them.
Source: PMC6456186 — systematic review of normal body temperature
Verbatim fragment: rectal mean 37.04 °C

Label: Mean 36.64 °C; mean ± 2 SD 35.76–37.52 °C
What it means / what to do: Measured mean is close to the oral mean, despite the '+0.6 °C' rule of thumb in some handbooks.
Verbatim fragment: tympanic is 36.64 degrees C (97.95 degrees F)
Note: Where the 'ear = oral + 0.6 °C' shortcut and the measured means disagree, this dataset keeps both and says so.

Label: Mean 35.97 °C; mean ± 2 SD 35.01–36.93 °C
What it means / what to do: A healthy adult armpit reading can legitimately be below 36 °C — so 'under 36' is not hypothermia.
Verbatim fragment: The average axillary temperature reading is 35.97 degrees C (96.75 degrees F)
Note: This row is the reason the dataset does not define a 36 °C hypothermia line.

Label: +0.6 °C (1.0 °F) vs oral
What it means / what to do: Add roughly 0.6 °C to an oral fever threshold when reading rectally.
Verbatim fragment: Rectal and tympanic membrane temperatures are about 0.6 °C higher than oral temperatures, whereas skin temperatures are about 0.6 °C lower.
Note: Merck gives one number (0.6 °C), not a 0.3–0.6 °C range; some patient leaflets give the range.

Label: +0.6 °C (1.0 °F) vs oral
What it means / what to do: Treat an ear reading as about 0.6 °C above an oral one, but expect wider scatter.
Verbatim fragment: Rectal and tympanic membrane temperatures are about 0.6 °C higher than oral temperatures
Note: The measured means in this dataset put ear and oral within 0.1 °C of each other — the two statements come from different kinds of source.

Label: −0.6 °C (1.0 °F) vs oral
What it means / what to do: Forehead and skin readings run low; Merck calls crystal/skin monitoring insensitive and not recommended for this purpose.
Verbatim fragment: whereas skin temperatures are about 0.6 °C lower
Note: NHS additionally warns that some infrared forehead devices do not meet UK regulations.

Label: 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher = fever
What it means / what to do: The public-health line most UK services use when telling you to act.
Verbatim fragment: A high temperature is usually considered to be 38C or above. This is sometimes called a fever.
Note: NHS publishes °C only; 100.4 °F is the exact conversion.

Label: Low-grade 37.3–38.0 °C (99.1–100.4 °F)
What it means / what to do: Clinically a fever band; not a 'call a doctor' threshold on its own.
Verbatim fragment: Low-grade: 37.3 to 38.0 C (99.1 to 100.4 F)
Note: Published fever bands are not the same cut-offs as the NHS/Mayo advice lines; both are in this dataset, each labelled.

Label: Moderate-grade 38.1–39.0 °C (100.6–102.2 °F)
What it means / what to do: Usually tolerated by a healthy adult; rest and fluids, watch the trend.
Verbatim fragment: Moderate-grade: 38.1 to 39.0 C (100.6 to 102.2 F)

Label: High-grade 39.1–41.0 °C (102.4–105.8 °F)
What it means / what to do: High-grade band in the clinical literature.
Verbatim fragment: High-grade: 39.1 to 41 C (102.4 to 105.8 F)

Label: Above 41.0 °C (105.8 °F)
What it means / what to do: StatPearls: hyperthermia/hyperpyrexia band — uncontrolled rise above the set-point; emergency.
Verbatim fragment: Hyperthermia: Greater than 41 C (105.8 F)
Note: Cleveland Clinic defines hyperpyrexia as above 106.7 °F (41.5 °C); the two cut-offs differ and both exist in the literature.

Label: Above 40.0 °C (104.0 °F) — or below 35.0 °C (95.0 °F)
What it means / what to do: Merck lists this as a red flag requiring immediate assessment.
Verbatim fragment: Temperature > 40° C or < 35° C

Label: 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher → seek care immediately
What it means / what to do: Do not wait for the fever to come down on your own; contact emergency services / go to A&E or the ER.
Verbatim fragment: is under 3 months old and has a temperature of 38C or higher
Note: AAP, Mayo Clinic and CDC publish the same 38.0 °C / 100.4 °F line for this age group; only the contact route differs (111 vs paediatrician vs ER).

Label: 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) or higher → contact a clinician the same day
What it means / what to do: NHS uses the 39 °C line specifically for the 3–6 month age band.
Verbatim fragment: is 3 to 6 months old and has a temperature of 39C or higher
Note: There is no single published 'children over 39 °C' rule: NHS ties 39 °C to 3–6 months, AAP uses 40 °C (104 °F), Mayo uses 38.9 °C (102 °F) rectal for 3–6 months.

Label: 39.4 °C (103 °F) or higher → call your health care provider
What it means / what to do: Mayo's adult number. NHS gives no adult temperature cut-off at all.
Source: Mayo Clinic — Fever (symptoms and when to see a doctor)
Verbatim fragment: Call your health care provider if your temperature is 103 F (39.4 C) or higher.
Note: US-style triage line; the page could not be re-fetched by script (403) — see provenance.

Label: Fever lasting more than 3 days → see a clinician
What it means / what to do: Duration triggers care independently of the number on the thermometer.
Verbatim fragment: stays at 103 F (39.4 C) or higher or lasts longer than three days
Note: Other published durations: NHS (children) 5 days; Merck 24–48 h for a phone call and 3–4 days for a visit. No single duration is universally agreed.

Label: Fever lasting 5 days or more → see a clinician
What it means / what to do: NHS threshold for children; also contact NHS 111 if the child is getting worse or you are worried.
Verbatim fragment: lasted for 5 days or more
Note: AAP uses more than 24 h under 2 years and more than 72 h at 2 years and over; Mayo uses 3 days.

Label: Below 35.0 °C (95.0 °F) → hypothermia, medical emergency
What it means / what to do: Call emergency services. Handle the person gently and keep them warm while help is on the way.
Source: StatPearls — Hypothermia; NHS — Hypothermia; CDC — Winter weather
Verbatim fragment: Hypothermia is defined as a decrease in body temperature below 35 °C.
Note: NHS: 'a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35C … It's a medical emergency'. CDC and Mayo use the same 95 °F / 35 °C line.

Label: Mild hypothermia 32.0–35.0 °C (90–95 °F)
What it means / what to do: Shivering, cognitive impairment; passive external rewarming is often sufficient in alert, stable patients.
Verbatim fragment: Patients with mild hypothermia have a core body temperature ranging from 32 to 35 °C (90 to 95 °F).
Note: Clinical staging for hospital care — not a home-triage tool.

Label: Moderate hypothermia 28.0–32.0 °C (82–90 °F)
What it means / what to do: Cognitive decline and lethargy; active rewarming under medical care.
Verbatim fragment: Patients with moderate hypothermia have a core body temperature of 28 to 32 °C (82-90 °F).

Label: Severe hypothermia below 28.0 °C (82.0 °F)
What it means / what to do: Risk of ventricular arrhythmias; hospital-level rewarming (up to ECMO / bypass).
Verbatim fragment: Individuals with severe hypothermia have a core body temperature of less than 28 °C (82 °F).

Label: 35.0–36.5 °C (95.0–97.7 °F) → below the usual range, not hypothermia
What it means / what to do: Recheck after 10 minutes, keep warm, and seek care if there are symptoms or the reading keeps falling.
Source: Derived: StatPearls hypothermia definition + measured axillary means
Verbatim fragment: The average axillary temperature reading is 35.97 degrees C
Note: No public-health source defines hypothermia at 36 °C, and the measured axillary mean in healthy adults is 35.97 °C — a 35.9 °C armpit reading is not a diagnosis.

Label: Perioperative: core temperature below 36.0 °C is 'low' and needs active management
What it means / what to do: This is a hospital quality threshold, not a layperson's hypothermia threshold.
Source: NICE CG65 — Hypothermia: prevention and management in adults having surgery
Verbatim fragment: core temperature below 36.0°C
Note: Included because this is where the widely-copied '36 °C = hypothermia' claim seems to come from.

Label: Paediatric inpatient: below 36.0 °C is treated as low temperature; neonates below 36.5 °C
What it means / what to do: Hospital escalation thresholds for children under inpatient care.
Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Temperature management
Verbatim fragment: paediatric low temperature (or hypothermia) <36 °C … neonates <36.5 °C
Note: Some NHS 111 regional triage pages likewise list 'temperature below 36 °C' as a sign to assess — the number is a care trigger in those settings, still not the definition.

Label: Newborn below 36.5 °C (97.7 °F) → warm and get help
What it means / what to do: Neonates are managed far more strictly than older children for cold readings.
Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Temperature management
Verbatim fragment: neonates <36.5 °C
Note: This is the one place where a threshold above 35 °C is genuinely the right safety line.

Label: Rash that does not fade under a glass
What it means / what to do: Emergency — call 999 / go to A&E, do not wait for the temperature to change.
Verbatim fragment: rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
Note: Emergency signs are listed without a temperature because no temperature is required to act.

Label: Stiff neck, dislike of bright light, severe headache
What it means / what to do: Emergency — these are the meningeal signs both NHS and Mayo list alongside fever.
Source: NHS — Fever in children; Mayo Clinic — Fever symptoms
Verbatim fragment: stiff neck and pain when you bend your head forward
Note: Quote is from Mayo's adult list; NHS lists 'stiff neck' and 'bothered by light' for children.

Label: A fit (febrile seizure) for the first time, or a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
What it means / what to do: Emergency. NHS lists a first fit as a 999/A&E sign; Mayo says call 911 if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes or recovery is not quick.
Source: NHS — Fever in children; Mayo Clinic — First aid: fever
Verbatim fragment: having a fit (febrile seizure) for the first time

Label: Blue / grey / pale / blotchy skin, cold hands and feet, drowsy and hard to wake
What it means / what to do: Emergency — circulatory and consciousness signs outrank the thermometer reading.
Verbatim fragment: skin colour changes (blue/grey/pale/blotchy)
Note: NHS also lists unusually cold hands and feet and being extremely agitated or confused in the same block.

Label: Difficulty breathing, breathlessness, breathing very fast, or chest pain
What it means / what to do: Emergency.
Source: NHS — Fever in children; Mayo Clinic — Fever symptoms
Verbatim fragment: difficulty breathing / breathlessness / breathing very fast

Label: Digital thermometer should reset below 35 °C (95 °F) before each reading
What it means / what to do: Practical check that the device can actually read the range that matters.
Verbatim fragment: Before each new measurement with a digital thermometer, the device should be reset to below 35 C (95 F).
